opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, mostly because I'm on the receiving end of a truly absurd number of them. Since I started doing more public stuff, mentoring people through programs like MATS and writing things online about getting into mechanistic interpretability, I get a steady stream of emails from people I've never met asking for advice, feedback, a call, or a research collaboration. So I've seen a huge sample of what works and what doesn't, and I can tell you from the inside what goes through a busy person's head when they open one.

And the patterns are really consistent. The ones I respond to are short, get to the point in the first line or two, make it clear exactly what they're asking for, and make that ask easy to say yes to. The ones I don't respond to are usually not bad people or bad ideas. They're just a wall of text where I'd have to do real work to figure out what they want, or the ask is vague, like "I'd love to pick your brain." When you have fifty emails in your inbox, anything that takes effort to parse just gets deferred, and deferred usually means never.

I've also been on the sending side a fair amount. Early in my career, cold emailing people was a big part of how I got opportunities, and it worked far better than I expected. So I have a decent sense of both sides: how much value a good cold email can unlock, and how much people underrate how easy it is to write one that actually gets read. That combination makes me feel like I'm not just speculating. I'm reporting what I see happening in my own inbox every week.

r001.rationale: He says he receives a steady stream of cold emails and has seen what works from the recipient’s perspective, which is why he feels confident giving advice.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is that I've just sent a lot of them, and I've been on the receiving end of a lot of them too. When I was starting out trying to get into alignment research, cold emailing people was basically my main strategy. I emailed researchers whose work I liked, I emailed people at labs, I emailed people who had written blog posts I thought were interesting, and a surprising fraction of them actually replied. Some of those replies turned into conversations, some turned into mentorship, and a couple of them turned into things that materially changed the trajectory of my career. So I have a pretty decent sample size of what worked and what got ignored.

And then the other side of it is that now I'm one of the people getting cold emailed. I get a lot of messages from people who want to get into mechanistic interpretability, want advice, want to collaborate, want me to look at something they've done. And I notice very quickly that there are emails I'm excited to respond to and emails I just never get around to, and the difference between them is often not about how impressive the person is. It's about whether the email makes it easy for me to say yes. Is it short? Is it clear what they actually want? Have they done the obvious bit of homework so I'm not explaining something that's on my website? Is there a specific, bounded ask rather than "can we have a chat sometime"?

So I don't think I have some deep theory of persuasion here. It's more that I've got a lot of data from both directions, and the patterns are pretty consistent. Most people's cold emails are much worse than they need to be, in fairly fixable ways, and the upside from fixing them is really high relative to the effort. That combination makes me fairly comfortable being opinionated about it.

r001.rationale: He says he now receives many cold emails and notices which ones he is excited to answer versus those he ignores, drawing on those observations when giving advice.

astra-6.text: I’ve been on both sides of this. I’ve sent cold emails that led to useful conversations and opportunities, and I now receive a lot of cold emails, so I get to notice what makes me want to respond. That gives me a useful perspective on where people go wrong. Obviously, my preferences aren’t universal, but I think some of the patterns generalise.

r001.rationale: He says he receives many cold emails and notices what makes him want to respond, grounding his advice in his own perceptions of them.

sol-6.1.text: I’ve been on both sides of this. I’ve sent a lot of cold emails, including ones that opened up really valuable opportunities for me, and I now receive quite a lot of them. So I get to see what makes me want to reply, what makes that easy, and what makes an email end up sitting in my inbox. That’s a pretty useful feedback loop. I wouldn’t claim to know what works for everyone, but I feel reasonably confident giving advice about emailing someone like me.

r001.rationale: He says he receives many cold emails and can see what makes him want to reply or leave an email sitting in his inbox, tying his confidence to his own perceptions of received emails.
